title: A Letter to the Founder Who Hasn't Told Anyone It's Bad

children: A Letter to the Founder Who Hasn't Told Anyone It's Bad
For the owner holding it together in public and falling apart in private, with what the 2026 data says about how many others are carrying the same weight.
Dear founder,
You haven't told anyone yet.

Not your team, because they need you steady. Not your spouse, at least not all of it, because they already worry. Not your friends, because they'd say "you'll figure it out" and then change the subject. So you carry it: the cash that's tighter than it looks, the customer who might leave, the partner who stopped pulling their weight, the number you check three times a day.
I want to say a few things you may not be hearing from anyone else. And because you're the kind of person who trusts numbers more than reassurance, I'll show you some of those, too.
You are far from the only one

It can feel like every other founder is doing fine. Their posts are full of wins, launches and hiring announcements. Yours would be, too, if you posted. But here's what founders say when someone asks them privately.
The weight behind the smile
In Bluevine's 2026 survey of 781 owners,
68% lose at least one full night of sleep a month
over money,
62% reduced or skipped their own pay
in the past year and
53% felt emotionally drained
by financial stress. In YouGov's research for the Start Up Loans Company,
55% of owners wish they had someone to turn to
So when you sit in your car for ten minutes before walking into the office, composing your face, you're not alone. You're in the majority. It's just a quiet majority.
First, this is normal

Not easy, but normal. Almost every business that has lasted went through a stretch exactly like this. The founders you admire had months when they couldn't sleep either; they just didn't post about it.
That doesn't make it smaller. It means it's survivable, and that there are people who've found their way through it.
Second, keeping it secret makes it heavier
Silence feels like protection. In reality, it removes every source of help. Problems that look impossible at 2 a.m. often look solvable after one honest conversation with someone who's been there.
There's also a practical cost. Decisions made in isolation tend to be delayed, distorted or hidden. Bluevine found
68% of owners delayed or avoided a major business decision
in the past year because of financial stress. The longer a hard decision waits, the more expensive it usually becomes.
Third, being "the strong one" is a role, not a requirement
Your team doesn't need you to be fearless. Instead, they need you to be honest enough to lead and steady enough to decide. You can be both while admitting you're not sure.

In fact, teams often handle the truth better than founders expect. "We had a hard quarter. Here's what we're doing about it, and here's what I need from you" builds more trust than a forced smile and a sudden round of cuts nobody saw coming.
Fourth, the decision you're avoiding is probably the one that matters
Usually there is one: a conversation, a cut, a price, a person. Avoiding it costs more every week. Making it, even imperfectly, gives you back the energy that avoidance is eating.

Try this. Write it down in one sentence. Then write what waiting is costing you each week, in money, energy or trust. Then write what information you're actually missing. If the answer to the last one is "nothing," the decision isn't blocked by information. It's blocked by discomfort. And discomfort is something people can help you carry.
Finally, you are more than this company
Your worth isn't the revenue line. If the business struggles, you haven't failed as a person; you're doing something genuinely hard.

It's easy to forget that when the business is your name, your savings and most of your waking hours. But the person who started this company had value before it existed and will have value whatever happens to it. Hold on to that person. They're going to need to make some good decisions soon, and they'll make them better if they're not also carrying shame.
What telling someone actually does
Telling someone helps
YouGov's research found that
59% of owners feel more connected when they know other leaders share their experiences
, and
74% say running their business has made them more resilient
. Yet only
38% actively connect with other business leaders
That gap, between how much founders benefit from connection and how few seek it, is where a lot of unnecessary suffering lives.

When you tell the right person, a few things happen. The problem gets smaller because it's out of your head and on the table. You hear that someone else survived something similar. You get one or two practical ideas you hadn't considered. And, often most importantly, you sleep a little better that night.
Who the "right person" is
Not everyone is the right person for this conversation. The right person:
Has run a business,
so they understand the weight without needing it explained.
Has nothing to sell you,
so their advice isn't tilted.
Will tell you the truth,
even when it's uncomfortable.
Will keep it confidential.
Will ask questions before giving answers.

That might be a former boss who started their own company, a founder you met years ago, a peer group or a structured community of founders. It's rarely your banker, your vendor or someone whose income depends on your decision.
What to say, if you don't know how to start
Sometimes the hardest part is the first sentence. Here are a few that work:
"Can I tell you something about the business I haven't said to anyone?"
"I'm stuck on a decision and I don't trust my own judgment on it right now. Can I walk you through it?"
"Things are harder than they look from the outside. I don't need you to fix it. I just need to say it."

You don't need to have a plan before you speak. You don't need to frame it perfectly. Founders who've been through hard seasons recognize the feeling immediately, and most are glad to be asked. Many will tell you it was a conversation exactly like this one that turned things around for them.
And if the first person you tell doesn't respond the way you hoped, try someone else. One unhelpful reaction doesn't mean asking was a mistake.
A small step for this week
Here's what I'd ask of you. Write down, in one sentence, what's actually wrong. Then tell one person who has run a business. Not to fix it; just to say it out loud.
If you don't have that person, find a room of them.

Frequently asked questions
Is it normal for founders to hide business problems?
Yes. Many founders hide stress from their teams, families and friends. 55% of owners say they wish they had someone to turn to, per YouGov research for the Start Up Loans Company.
How many business owners lose sleep over money?
68% lose at least one full night of sleep a month due to financial worries, according to Bluevine's 2026 research.
Why does keeping business problems secret make them worse?
Isolation removes outside input, which leads to delayed and distorted decisions. Bluevine found 68% of owners delayed or avoided a major decision because of financial stress.
Who should a founder talk to about business struggles?
Someone who has run a business, has nothing to sell, will tell the truth and will keep it confidential, such as an experienced founder or a structured founder community.
Where can founders find a confidential peer community?
The Lonely Entrepreneur's Learning Community offers group coaching, weekly sessions with Michael Dermer and a community of founders at similar stages.
